qPCR: Real-time monitoring of amplification using fluorescent dyes (SYBR Green) or probes (TaqMan). Quantitative. Used for viral load measurement and gene expression.
Multiplex PCR: Multiple primer pairs in one reaction. Amplifies several targets simultaneously. Used in forensic STR profiling and multi-pathogen panels.
Nested PCR: Two sequential PCRs. Outer primers first, then inner (nested) primers on the product. Highest sensitivity and specificity for low-copy targets.
Applications: Medical diagnosis (COVID, HIV), forensics (DNA fingerprinting), genetic disorders (cystic fibrosis), gene cloning, animal biotechnology, archaeological DNA.
Limitations: Prior sequence knowledge needed. Contamination causes false positives. Taq errors (no proofreading). Non-specific bands if Mg²⁺ or annealing T not optimised.
Primers: 18–25 nt synthetic oligos. Two required: forward + reverse. Complementary to template flanking the target. Annealing T = Tm − 5°C. Define the amplicon.

sa.q: What is PCR? Explain its principle and the three stages of a PCR cycle.
sa.a: Definition: Polymerase Chain Reaction — in vitro exponential amplification of a specific DNA segment using thermal cycling. Invented by Kary Mullis (1983); Nobel Prize 1993. Principle: repeated cycles of denaturation → annealing → extension; each cycle doubles copies; exponential amplification = 2ⁿ after n cycles. Stage 1 — Denaturation: 94–96°C; H-bonds broken; dsDNA → 2 ssDNA templates. Stage 2 — Annealing: 50–65°C; primers (forward + reverse) bind complementary template sequences; Tm−5°C rule. Stage 3 — Extension: 72°C; Taq polymerase adds dNTPs 5'→3' from primers; rate ~1000 bp/min. After 30–40 cycles → ~10⁶–10⁹ copies. Include a diagram of the temperature cycle.

sa.q: What are the components required for PCR? State the function of each.
sa.a: Template DNA — source DNA with target sequence. Primers (×2, forward + reverse) — define amplicon; 18–25 nt; provide 3'-OH for extension. Taq DNA polymerase — heat-stable; from T. aquaticus; synthesises new strand at 72°C. dNTPs (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP) — building blocks for DNA synthesis. PCR buffer (Tris-HCl, KCl) — maintains optimal pH 8.3–8.8. MgCl₂ (1.5–2.5 mM) — essential polymerase cofactor; stabilises primer-template duplexes. Thermal cycler — automated temperature control. Exam tip: Know the role of Mg²⁺ separately — it's frequently asked alone.

sa.q: What is RT-PCR? How does it differ from conventional PCR and what are its applications?
sa.a: RT-PCR = Reverse Transcriptase PCR. Uses RNA as starting material, not DNA. Key step: RNA → cDNA by reverse transcriptase (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase) BEFORE PCR. Two-step process: (1) RT step: mRNA + oligo-dT primer + RT enzyme → cDNA; (2) PCR: cDNA amplified by standard thermal cycling. Difference from conventional PCR: conventional uses DNA template directly; RT-PCR requires reverse transcription first to convert RNA to cDNA. Applications: detection of RNA viruses (SARS-CoV-2, HIV, influenza); gene expression analysis; transcriptome studies. COVID-19 diagnosis: RT-qPCR combines reverse transcription + real-time PCR.

sa.q: What is exponential amplification in PCR? Calculate the number of copies after 20 cycles.
sa.a: Exponential amplification: each cycle doubles the target DNA, so copies increase as powers of 2. Formula: Number of copies = 2ⁿ (where n = number of cycles starting from 1 molecule). After 20 cycles: 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 ≈ 1 million copies. After 30 cycles: 2³⁰ ≈ 1.07 × 10⁹ ≈ 1 billion copies. Why exponential? Because products of each cycle serve as templates in the next cycle — not just the original two strands. Practical note: efficiency is not 100% in real reactions, so actual yield is somewhat lower (typically 80–90% efficiency per cycle).

sa.q: Describe the applications of PCR in medical diagnosis, forensics, and animal biotechnology.
sa.a: Medical diagnosis: RT-PCR detects RNA viruses (SARS-CoV-2 → COVID-19, HIV, hepatitis C); conventional PCR detects bacterial pathogens (M. tuberculosis, Chlamydia); multiplex PCR panels detect multiple pathogens in one test. Genetic disorder analysis: Detects mutations in CFTR (cystic fibrosis), HBB (sickle cell), BRCA1/2 (breast cancer); prenatal diagnosis from amniotic fluid cells. Forensic science: STR profiling by multiplex PCR from blood, hair, skin cells at crime scenes; DNA fingerprinting for identification; paternity testing. Animal biotechnology: Sex determination of embryos (SRY gene); detection of transgene integration in transgenic animals; breed/species identification; detection of animal pathogens; quality control of animal products. Gene cloning: Amplifies gene of interest for cloning into vector; colony PCR confirms successful insertion.

gl.d: An in vitro technique for amplifying a specific DNA segment exponentially using repeated thermal cycling steps (denaturation, annealing, extension) and a thermostable DNA polymerase. Invented by Kary Mullis in 1983.
The source DNA containing the target sequence to be amplified in PCR. Can be genomic DNA, cDNA, plasmid DNA, or forensic/clinical samples. Typically used in nanogram quantities per reaction.

A short (18–25 nt) synthetic single-stranded oligonucleotide complementary to the template flanking the target region. Two primers are required: forward (sense) and reverse (antisense). Defines the exact boundaries of the amplified product (amplicon).
The first stage of each PCR cycle. Heating to 94–96°C breaks hydrogen bonds between base pairs, separating the double-stranded DNA into single-stranded templates for primer binding in the next step.

The second stage of each PCR cycle (50–65°C). Primers hybridise to their complementary sequences on the single-stranded template through Watson-Crick base pairing. Annealing temperature = Tm − 5°C of the primers.
The third stage of each PCR cycle (72°C). Taq DNA polymerase extends each primer by adding dNTPs complementary to the template in the 5'→3' direction, synthesising a new complementary DNA strand.

A thermostable DNA polymerase isolated from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium from hot springs. Withstands the 94–96°C denaturation step of PCR. Optimal activity at 72°C. Rate: ~1000 bp/min. Lacks 3'→5' proofreading exonuclease activity.

A programmable device that automatically and precisely controls the temperature cycling of PCR reactions. Alternates between the denaturation, annealing, and extension temperatures for the programmed number of cycles, enabling complete automation of PCR.

The PCR product — the double-stranded DNA fragment amplified between (and including) the two primer sequences. Its size is fixed by the primer positions and is detected as a band on agarose gel electrophoresis.

RNA-dependent DNA polymerase from retroviruses (e.g., MMLV-RT). In RT-PCR, converts single-stranded mRNA into complementary DNA (cDNA) before PCR amplification. Essential for detecting and studying RNA targets including RNA viruses.

protein_databases_app.html.title: Protein Databases: SWISS-PROT, UniProt & PDB
kp: SWISS-PROT: erland / 🇺🇸 USA · SIB & EBI SWISS-PROT — The Manually Curated Protein Sequence Database SWISS-PROT is a manually reviewed, non-redundant protein sequence database that provides high-quality annotation for each entry. It was established in 1986 at the Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics (SIB) by Amos Bairoch and is now maintained jointly by SIB and the European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI) as part of UniProt.
Nucleotide databases (GenBank, EMBL) store DNA/RNA sequences; protein sequence databases (SWISS-PROT, UniProt) store amino acid sequences; structural databases (PDB) store 3D atomic coordinates.
SWISS-PROT: manually reviewed, non-redundant protein sequence database; founded 1986 by Amos Bairoch; maintained by SIB + EBI; now the reviewed tier of UniProt.
UniProt: comprehensive protein resource created 2002; UniProtKB = Swiss-Prot (reviewed, ~570K) + TrEMBL (unreviewed, ~220M entries).
SWISS-PROT is a subset of UniProt — all Swiss-Prot entries are in UniProt, but UniProt contains far more entries.
PDB (Protein Data Bank): world's only archive of 3D macromolecular structures; founded 1971; managed by wwPDB; stores atomic XYZ coordinates, experimental method, ligands.
PDB methods: X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy, Cryo-EM. Each structure has a unique 4-character PDB ID (e.g., 1HHO for haemoglobin).
Data flow: lab → database entry → storage → retrieval → analysis/application.
Applications: protein ID (UniProt), functional annotation (Swiss-Prot), drug design (PDB), evolutionary studies (both), disease research (both).
AlphaFold 2 (2021) predicted structures for nearly all human proteins — linking sequence (UniProt) and structure (PDB) databases.

sa.q: What is SWISS-PROT? Describe its features and importance as a protein sequence database.
sa.a: Define SWISS-PROT (manually reviewed, non-redundant protein sequence database; founded 1986 by Amos Bairoch; SIB + EBI; now part of UniProt). Features: manual expert curation, non-redundant entries, rich annotation (sequence, function, PTMs, disease, organism), cross-references to 100+ databases. Importance: gold standard for protein data quality; preferred for reliable biological interpretation; widely cited in molecular biology research.

sa.q: Explain UniProt and its components. What is the relationship between SWISS-PROT and UniProt?
sa.a: UniProt = Universal Protein Resource; created 2002 by SIB + EBI + PIR. Components: UniProtKB (central knowledgebase = Swiss-Prot + TrEMBL), UniRef (sequence clusters), UniParc (archive). Swiss-Prot vs TrEMBL: Swiss-Prot (~570K) = manually reviewed ("gold standard"); TrEMBL (~220M) = computationally annotated, awaiting review. Relationship: SWISS-PROT is a subset (reviewed tier) of UniProt. TrEMBL entries graduate to Swiss-Prot after expert review.

sa.q: What is the Protein Data Bank (PDB)? Describe the type of data it stores and its importance in structural biology.
sa.a: PDB = Protein Data Bank; founded 1971; managed by wwPDB (RCSB, PDBe, PDBj). Data stored: 3D atomic XYZ coordinates (in Å), amino acid/nucleotide sequence, experimental method (X-ray, NMR, Cryo-EM), resolution, ligands, biological assembly. Importance: reveals how proteins fold and function; essential for rational/structure-based drug design; HIV protease inhibitors and COVID-19 antivirals designed using PDB data; training data for AI structure prediction (AlphaFold).

sa.q: Distinguish between protein sequence databases and structural databases. Give two examples of each type.
sa.a: Protein sequence databases: store 1D amino acid sequences + annotations; tell you WHAT the protein is made of; examples: SWISS-PROT, UniProt (UniProtKB). Structural databases: store 3D atomic coordinates; tell you WHAT SHAPE the protein adopts; examples: PDB, AlphaFold Database. Key distinction: a protein can have a known sequence but unknown structure — not all UniProt proteins are in PDB. Structural data requires laborious experimental methods; sequence data is more easily obtained.

sa.q: Discuss the applications of protein and structural databases in biotechnology and drug research.
sa.a: Applications: (1) Protein identification — BLAST search against UniProt/Swiss-Prot; (2) Functional annotation — retrieve known function without lab experiments; (3) Drug design — PDB active site visualisation, molecular docking, virtual screening; (4) Disease research — Swiss-Prot variant annotations; (5) Evolutionary studies — phylogenetic trees from retrieved sequences; (6) Industrial enzymes — search for thermostable or pH-tolerant homologues; (7) Structure prediction validation (AlphaFold vs PDB). Mention specific examples: HIV protease inhibitors, COVID-19 antivirals.

gl.d: The linear order of amino acids in a polypeptide chain (primary structure); determines the protein's identity and, ultimately, its 3D shape and function.
A manually reviewed, non-redundant protein sequence database; the "gold standard" for protein annotation; founded 1986; now the reviewed tier of UniProt.
Universal Protein Resource — the world's most comprehensive protein database, containing UniProtKB (Swiss-Prot + TrEMBL), UniRef, and UniParc; created 2002.
A database in which entries have been manually reviewed and verified by expert scientists — ensuring accuracy but limiting speed and scale.
Biological information added to a sequence or structure entry — protein name, function, subcellular location, post-translational modifications, disease links.
Protein Data Bank — the world's only archive of three-dimensional structures of biological macromolecules; stores atomic XYZ coordinates determined by X-ray, NMR, or Cryo-EM.
The complete spatial arrangement of all atoms in a macromolecule — the tertiary (and quaternary) structure. Stored in PDB as XYZ coordinates in Ångströms.
The branch of molecular biology that studies the molecular structure of biological macromolecules and how structure relates to function.
The biological role a protein performs — enzymatic catalysis, structural support, signalling, transport, or regulation.
The unreviewed tier of UniProtKB — automatically annotated protein sequences from genome sequencing projects; entries await manual curation to graduate to Swiss-Prot.
A unique 4-character alphanumeric identifier assigned to each structure deposited in the Protein Data Bank (e.g., 1HHO for haemoglobin).
Cryo-Electron Microscopy — an experimental technique for determining 3D structures of macromolecules at near-atomic resolution, particularly useful for large complexes.

sanger_dna_sequencing.html.title: DNA Sequencing: Sanger Method
kp: Sanger Method: Developed by Frederick Sanger in 1977 (Nobel Prize 1980). Also called chain-termination or dideoxy method. The gold standard for DNA sequencing.
Key Principle: Uses ddNTPs as chain terminators. ddNTPs lack a 3'-OH group → when incorporated, chain synthesis stops permanently.
dNTP vs ddNTP: Only structural difference: dNTP has 3'-OH; ddNTP has 3'-H (no OH). This single difference prevents the next phosphodiester bond formation.
Fragment Ladder: Reaction produces fragments of all possible lengths, each ending at a specific nucleotide type. Reading fragment sizes in order reveals the sequence.
dNTP:ddNTP Ratio: ddNTPs are ~100× more dilute than dNTPs to ensure random incorporation at every position — producing the complete ladder of fragment sizes.
Original Method: Four separate reactions (ddA, ddT, ddG, ddC), radioactive labelling, 4-lane polyacrylamide gel, read bottom to top, autoradiography.
Modern Method: Single reaction, four fluorescently labelled ddNTPs (each different colour), capillary electrophoresis, chromatogram output, automated base calling.
Gel Reading: Read bottom to top (smallest = earliest position). Each band's lane/colour = the nucleotide at that position. Sequence is the new strand read 5'→3'.
Read Length & Accuracy: 600–1000 reliable bases per run; >99.99% accuracy for high-quality bases. First 15–40 bases may be unreliable.
Applications: Clone verification, mutation detection, Human Genome Project, clinical diagnostics, pathogen identification, forensics.

Limitation vs NGS: Only ~1 kb per reaction (low throughput); expensive for whole genomes. NGS sequences billions of bases simultaneously but Sanger remains gold standard for accuracy in targeted sequencing.
Correct Step Order: Denature DNA → Anneal primer → Polymerase extends + ddNTP terminates → Fragments of all sizes form → Electrophoresis separates → Read sequence from chromatogram.

sa.q: What is the principle of Sanger's chain termination method of DNA sequencing?
sa.a: Principle: chain-termination (dideoxy method) using dideoxynucleotide triphosphates (ddNTPs) as chain terminators. ddNTPs are structural analogues of normal dNTPs but lack a 3'-OH group (have 3'-H instead). DNA polymerase incorporates ddNTPs into the growing chain at random positions — when ddNTP is incorporated, no further elongation is possible (no 3'-OH for next phosphodiester bond). This produces a population of fragments of all possible lengths, each starting at the primer and ending at a specific base type. Separation by electrophoresis and reading the positions gives the complete sequence. Developed by Frederick Sanger in 1977 (Nobel Prize Chemistry 1980).

sa.q: Why does the incorporation of a dideoxynucleotide (ddNTP) cause chain termination? Explain with reference to its structure.
sa.a: Normal dNTP has: 5'-triphosphate, deoxyribose sugar with 2'-H and 3'-OH, and a nucleobase. ddNTP differs in ONE critical way: the 3' position of the deoxyribose sugar has a hydrogen atom (3'-H) instead of a hydroxyl group (3'-OH). DNA polymerase extends a chain by catalysing an attack of the 3'-OH on the α-phosphate of the incoming dNTP, forming a new 3'–5' phosphodiester bond and releasing pyrophosphate. When a ddNTP is incorporated: its 5'-phosphate forms a bond with the previous nucleotide's 3'-OH. But the ddNTP itself now sits at the 3' end with only a 3'-H — no hydroxyl group is available to attack the next incoming nucleotide. Therefore, no new phosphodiester bond can form → synthesis is permanently halted → chain termination. Include a structural diagram comparing dNTP and ddNTP showing the 3'-OH vs 3'-H difference.

sa.q: Describe the steps involved in Sanger DNA sequencing. How is the sequence determined from the result?
sa.a: Step 1: Denature template DNA to single strands (heat or NaOH). Step 2: Anneal oligonucleotide primer to template (50–60°C). Step 3: Add DNA polymerase, all four dNTPs, and all four fluorescently labelled ddNTPs (100× lower concentration than dNTPs). Step 4: Synthesis proceeds; at each position, ddNTP may be randomly incorporated → chain terminates at every possible position → population of fragments of all lengths is produced. Step 5: Fragments denatured and loaded into capillary electrophoresis instrument. Step 6: Fragments separated by size; laser detects fluorescent colour as each fragment elutes. Sequence determination: chromatogram shows coloured peaks; each colour = one base; peaks read left to right (small = earliest in 5'→3' sequence).

sa.q: What is the role of dNTPs and ddNTPs in Sanger sequencing? Why are ddNTPs added at a much lower concentration than dNTPs?
sa.a: Role of dNTPs: Normal building blocks — provide the nucleotide subunits for DNA chain elongation. All four (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP) are needed. Their 3'-OH groups allow the chain to continue growing. Role of ddNTPs: Chain terminators — incorporated randomly at complementary positions and permanently stop synthesis. Each one terminates at a specific base type. In modern sequencing, each carries a different fluorescent dye for base identification. Why low concentration of ddNTPs? If ddNTPs were in equal or higher concentration, almost every fragment would be very short (terminated near the primer). A low ddNTP:dNTP ratio (~1:100) ensures that termination occurs rarely and randomly across the entire length of the template — generating fragments of every possible length from position 1 to ~1000 nt. This complete "ladder" of fragment sizes is essential for reading the full sequence.

sa.q: List the components required for Sanger sequencing. State the advantages and limitations of this method.
sa.a: Components: (1) Template DNA (single-stranded); (2) Primer (specific oligonucleotide); (3) DNA polymerase (Klenow fragment, T7, or Taq); (4) All four dNTPs (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP); (5) All four ddNTPs (ddATP, ddTTP, ddGTP, ddCTP — each fluorescently labelled); (6) Buffer with Mg²⁺ cofactor. Advantages: High accuracy (>99.99%); long reads (600–1000 bp); gold standard; automated; cost-effective for single genes. Limitations: Low throughput (only ~1 kb per reaction); expensive for whole genomes; first 15–40 bases unreliable; cannot sequence repetitive regions well; requires pure single-sequence template. Brief mention of NGS as higher-throughput alternative, but Sanger remains preferred for targeted, high-accuracy sequencing.

gl.d: The process of determining the precise order of nucleotide bases (A, T, G, C) along a DNA strand. The sequence reveals the genetic information encoded in the DNA molecule.

A DNA sequencing technique developed by Frederick Sanger in 1977, based on the chain-termination principle using dideoxynucleotides. Also called the dideoxy method. Gold standard of DNA sequencing for over 30 years.

A synthetic analogue of a normal deoxyribonucleotide triphosphate (dNTP), lacking a 3'-OH group (replaced by 3'-H). When incorporated by DNA polymerase, it permanently terminates chain elongation. Used as chain terminators in Sanger sequencing.
The permanent halting of DNA synthesis caused by incorporation of a ddNTP. Since ddNTPs lack a 3'-OH group, no new phosphodiester bond can be formed — the growing chain cannot be extended further.

The single-stranded DNA molecule used as the blueprint in DNA synthesis. In Sanger sequencing, the template strand is read 3'→5' by DNA polymerase, which synthesises a new complementary strand in the 5'→3' direction.

A short (18–25 nt) synthetic single-stranded oligonucleotide complementary to the template strand. Provides the free 3'-OH required for DNA polymerase to initiate synthesis. Defines the start and direction of sequencing in Sanger method.

A technique that uses an electric field to separate charged molecules (such as DNA fragments) by size. Smaller fragments migrate faster and farther in the gel or capillary. Enables single-nucleotide resolution of Sanger sequencing fragments.

The graphical output of automated fluorescent Sanger sequencing showing coloured peaks on a time axis. Each peak represents one nucleotide — the peak colour identifies the base (A/T/G/C) and peak position reflects fragment size.

A modern, automated separation method used in Sanger sequencing where DNA fragments migrate through a thin polymer-filled capillary tube. Laser detection of fluorescence allows high-resolution, high-throughput sequencing (e.g., ABI 3730xl platform).
Deoxynucleoside triphosphate — the normal building block of DNA. Contains a deoxyribose sugar with a free 3'-OH group that allows continued chain elongation. Four types: dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP.

screening_selection_recombinants.html.title: Screening & Selection of Recombinants
kp: Need for Screening: After transformation, all colony types look identical. Selection/screening is essential to identify cells with the correct recombinant vector among transformed and non-transformed cells.
Selection vs Screening: Selection = cells either survive or die (antibiotic). Screening = all cells survive but a signal distinguishes recombinants (colour, probe signal).
Direct Selection: Antibiotic resistance on vector. Only transformants survive. Does NOT distinguish recombinant from non-recombinant. FIRST step always.
Insertional Inactivation: pBR322 example. Insert into BamHI site disrupts tet^r. Recombinants: amp^r, tet^s. Identified by replica plating. Recombinants absent from tet plate.
Blue-White Selection: pUC19 vector. Insert in MCS disrupts lacZ-α. Blue = non-recombinant (lacZ intact, X-gal cleaved). White = recombinant (lacZ disrupted). Needs X-gal + IPTG in medium.
Colony Hybridization: Most specific method. Labelled probe hybridises to target gene. Steps: colony blot → lysis (NaOH) → DNA fixation → probe → wash → autoradiograph → pick from master plate.
X-gal: Colourless β-galactosidase substrate. Cleaved by intact β-gal → blue compound. NOT an antibiotic — a chromogenic substrate.
IPTG: Non-hydrolysable lac operon inducer. Ensures lacZ-α is expressed for blue-white screening. NOT an antibiotic — a transcriptional inducer.
pBR322 vs pUC19: pBR322 → insertional inactivation (two antibiotic genes: amp^r + tet^r). pUC19 → blue-white selection (lacZ-α + MCS). Both also used with direct antibiotic selection.
Probe in Colony Hybridization: ³²P-labelled ssDNA or RNA. Complementary to gene of interest. After hybridisation and washing, positive colonies detected by autoradiography on X-ray film.

α-Complementation: In blue-white, the vector supplies lacZ-α fragment and the host (DH5α, JM109) supplies lacZ-ω. Together they form active β-galactosidase. Insert disrupts α-peptide → no complementation → white colony.

Correct Workflow Order: Transform → plate on antibiotic (direct selection) → screen for recombinant (blue-white or insertional inactivation) → confirm with colony hybridization or PCR → verify by sequencing.

sa.q: What is the difference between selection and screening in the context of gene cloning? Give one example of each.
sa.a: Selection: An active process where only cells with the desired property survive on selective medium; non-selected cells are eliminated. Example: plating transformed E. coli on ampicillin — only cells with the vector (carrying amp^r gene) survive; non-transformed cells die. Screening: A passive process where all cells survive, but a detectable signal (colour, probe signal) allows identification of cells with the desired property without killing others. Example: blue-white screening — all transformants survive, but recombinants form white colonies while non-recombinants form blue colonies. Key difference: selection = growth/no growth; screening = identifying among surviving colonies. Selection is always step 1 (reduces to transformants); screening is step 2 (identifies recombinants among transformants).

sa.q: Describe insertional inactivation using pBR322. How are recombinant clones identified?
sa.a: pBR322 has two antibiotic resistance genes: amp^r and tet^r. The tet^r gene contains unique restriction sites BamHI, SalI, and ClaI. When the gene of interest is cloned into the BamHI site (within tet^r), the tet^r gene is disrupted → recombinant cells become tetracycline-sensitive. After transformation, cells are plated on LB + ampicillin → all transformants (both recombinant and non-recombinant) grow. Replica plating to LB + tetracycline: non-recombinants (intact tet^r) grow on both plates; recombinants (disrupted tet^r) grow only on amp plate — ABSENT on tet plate. Recombinants identified as colonies present on amp plate but absent on tet plate. These are picked from the original amp master plate. Result: amp^r, tet^s = recombinant. amp^r, tet^r = non-recombinant.

sa.q: Explain blue-white selection. Why are white colonies considered recombinants in this system?
sa.a: Blue-white selection uses pUC vectors (e.g., pUC19) that carry the lacZ-α gene with the MCS inserted within it. Medium: LB + ampicillin (to select transformants) + X-gal (chromogenic substrate for β-gal) + IPTG (lac operon inducer). Without insert: lacZ-α is intact → IPTG induces expression → functional β-galactosidase α-peptide produced (by α-complementation with host lacZ-ω) → β-gal cleaves X-gal → blue compound → BLUE colony = non-recombinant. With insert in MCS: lacZ-α reading frame is disrupted → no functional α-peptide → no α-complementation → β-gal cannot cleave X-gal → no blue compound → colony remains WHITE = recombinant. Therefore, white colonies have an insert disrupting lacZ → they are recombinant transformants. White ≠ necessarily has the correct insert — further confirmation needed (PCR, restriction analysis, sequencing).

sa.q: Describe the steps involved in colony hybridization for identifying recombinant colonies.
sa.a: 1. Colony transfer: Replica nylon/nitrocellulose membrane placed on master plate — colonies adhere; membrane peeled off. Keep master plate as reference. 2. Cell lysis: Membrane treated with NaOH — cells lyse, DNA released and denatured into single strands. 3. DNA fixation: Membrane baked at 80°C (2 hrs) or UV-cross-linked — single-stranded DNA permanently immobilised on membrane. 4. Pre-hybridisation (blocking): Non-specific sites blocked with salmon sperm DNA/BSA to reduce background. 5. Probe hybridisation: ³²P-labelled ssDNA probe (complementary to gene of interest) added. Probe anneals only to complementary target sequences at appropriate stringency. 6. Washing: Non-specifically bound probe washed off with increasing stringency washes. 7. Detection: Membrane exposed to X-ray film (autoradiography) — positive colonies appear as dark spots. 8. Identification: Alignment marks used to match positive spots on film to corresponding colonies on master plate. Positive colonies picked for further analysis.

sa.q: Compare insertional inactivation and blue-white selection as methods of screening recombinants. Which is more convenient and why?
sa.a: Insertional Inactivation: Vector pBR322. Insert disrupts tet^r at BamHI site. Recombinants: amp^r, tet^s. Identified by REPLICA PLATING (negative result — absent from tet plate). Two plates needed. Takes 2 days. No special reagents. Blue-White Selection: Vector pUC19. Insert disrupts lacZ-α at MCS. Recombinants: white colonies. Non-recombinants: blue colonies. Identified on SAME plate (positive visual result). One plate, one step. Requires X-gal + IPTG. Blue-white is more convenient because: (a) results visible on the same plate without replica plating; (b) positive visual identification (white = recombinant) vs negative identification (absent from tet plate); (c) faster (overnight); (d) less technically demanding. Both are used after direct antibiotic selection; neither confirms the CORRECT insert — only that some insert is present. Colony hybridization is still needed to confirm the specific gene.

gl.d: A cell or organism containing foreign DNA that has been introduced into its genome or as an episomal element. In gene cloning, a recombinant clone is a bacterial colony carrying a vector with the gene of interest inserted into its MCS.

A gene (typically an antibiotic resistance gene) on a cloning vector used to identify transformed host cells. Only cells expressing the marker gene survive on selective medium. Examples: amp^r, kan^r, tet^r, neo^r.

The disruption of a marker gene's function by inserting foreign DNA into a restriction site within it. Used to distinguish recombinant (marker-inactive) from non-recombinant (marker-active) transformants. Classic example: pBR322 tet^r disrupted by insert at BamHI site.

The E. coli gene encoding β-galactosidase. In pUC vectors, the lacZ-α fragment (with MCS within it) is used for blue-white screening. An insert in the MCS disrupts lacZ-α → no functional β-galactosidase → colony remains white (recombinant).

5-Bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl-β-D-galactopyranoside. A colourless chromogenic substrate for β-galactosidase. Cleavage by active β-gal releases a blue insoluble compound (5-bromo-4-chloro-indigo), producing blue colonies in blue-white screening.

Isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside. A non-metabolisable inducer of the E. coli lac operon. Induces expression of lacZ-α in pUC vectors during blue-white screening, ensuring sufficient β-galactosidase production for a visible blue signal.

A labelled single-stranded DNA or RNA molecule complementary to a specific target sequence. Used in colony hybridization to identify colonies containing the gene of interest by sequence-specific base pairing. Labelled with ³²P, digoxigenin, or biotin.

A molecular screening technique where bacterial colonies are transferred to a membrane, lysed, DNA denatured and fixed, and then probed with a labelled nucleic acid probe. Positive colonies (hybridised to probe) are detected by autoradiography and picked from the master plate.

A technique for making an exact copy of colony positions from one plate to another, using a sterile velvet pad. Used in insertional inactivation to compare growth on ampicillin vs tetracycline plates to identify recombinants (absent on tet plate = amp^r, tet^s).

The reconstitution of functional β-galactosidase by combining the lacZ-α peptide (from pUC vector) with the lacZ-ω peptide (from host strain). An insert in the MCS disrupts lacZ-α → no complementation → no functional β-gal → white colony (recombinant).

animal_cell_culture.html.title: Animal Cell Culture Techniques
kp: Animal cell culture: growth of cells isolated from animal tissue in vitro under controlled temperature (37 °C), pH (7.2–7.4), CO₂ (5–10%) and nutrition.
Milestones: Harrison 1907 (nerve fibre culture); Earle 1943 (mouse fibroblast line); HeLa 1951 (first immortal human line); hybridoma 1975; human ES cells 1998; iPSC 2006 (Yamanaka).

Sterilisation: autoclave 121 °C, 15 psi, 15–20 min (media, glassware); dry heat 160–170 °C (glassware); 0.22 µm filtration for serum and heat-labile media; 70% ethanol for surfaces; UV 254 nm in the cabinet.
pH is monitored with phenol red (yellow = acidic) and buffered by bicarbonate (with CO₂) or HEPES; osmolarity 280–320 mOsm/kg.
Media: natural (plasma, serum, tissue extracts, embryo extract) and synthetic (DMEM, RPMI 1640, MEM, Ham’s F12); serum-free and protein-free media remove batch variability and contamination risk.
Primary culture: cells taken directly from tissue (mechanical or enzymatic dissociation with trypsin or collagenase); finite life span, heterogeneous; explant versus monolayer.
Trypan blue exclusion: live cells stay clear, dead cells stain blue; viability should be ≥ 90% before seeding.
Subculture (passage) of adherent cells: PBS wash, trypsin-EDTA, neutralise with serum medium, split 1:3 to 1:10; normal cells are finite (Hayflick limit, ~50 divisions).
Continuous lines: HeLa (cervical carcinoma), CHO (hamster ovary, biopharmaceuticals), Vero (monkey kidney, vaccines), NIH 3T3, MCF-7, Jurkat, PC12.
Cryopreservation: ~10% DMSO, cool at −1 °C/min, store in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C; thaw rapidly at 37 °C and dilute the DMSO.
Stem cells: ESC (pluripotent, from inner cell mass), iPSC (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc), HSC (CD34⁺, bone-marrow transplant), MSC (osteoblasts, chondrocytes, adipocytes), NSC (neurospheres).
Organ culture preserves 3-D architecture: watch-glass (Fell and Robison), grid/raft, perfusion and roller-tube methods.
Artificial skin: keratinocytes + fibroblasts on a collagen scaffold, air–liquid interface for stratification; Apligraf, Integra, Epicel, Dermagraft; limits: no vessels, nerves or glands.

sa.q: Define animal cell culture and mention its applications.
sa.a: Growth of cells removed from an animal in vitro under controlled temperature, pH, CO₂ and nutrition. Applications: vaccine and biopharmaceutical production, cancer biology, drug screening, genetic engineering, tissue engineering and virology.
sa.q_ta: விலங்கு செல் வளர்ப்பை வரையறுத்து, அதன் பயன்பாடுகளைக் குறிப்பிடுக.
sa.a_ta: விலங்கிலிருந்து எடுத்த செல்களைக் கட்டுப்படுத்தப்பட்ட வெப்பநிலை, pH, CO₂, ஊட்டச்சத்து ஆகியவற்றின் கீழ் இன் விட்ரோ-வில் வளர்த்தல். பயன்பாடுகள்: தடுப்பூசி, உயிர்மருந்து உற்பத்தி, புற்றுநோய் உயிரியல், மருந்துச் சலிக்கை, மரபணுப் பொறியியல், திசுப் பொறியியல், வைரஸ் ஆய்வியல்.

sa.q: List the basic requirements for animal cell culture.
sa.a: Physical: 37 °C, pH 7.2–7.4, 5–10% CO₂, ≥95% humidity. Chemical: basal medium (DMEM/RPMI) with serum or defined supplements. Biological: correct inoculum density and timely subculture. Sterility: biosafety cabinet, antibiotics, aseptic technique.
sa.q_ta: விலங்கு செல் வளர்ப்புக்கான அடிப்படைத் தேவைகளைப் பட்டியலிடுக.
sa.a_ta: இயற்பியல்: 37 °C, pH 7.2–7.4, 5–10% CO₂, ≥95% ஈரப்பதம். வேதியியல்: சீரம் அல்லது வரையறுக்கப்பட்ட துணைப்பொருள்களுடன் அடிப்படை ஊடகம் (DMEM/RPMI). உயிரியல்: சரியான உட்செலுத்து அடர்த்தி, உரிய நேரத்தில் துணை வளர்ப்பு. நுண்ணுயிர் நீக்கம்: உயிர்ப் பாதுகாப்புப் பெட்டி, நுண்ணுயிர்க்கொல்லிகள், கிருமியற்ற நுட்பம்.

sa.q: Differentiate natural and synthetic media.
sa.a: Natural media are biological fluids (plasma, serum, tissue extracts, embryo extract); they are rich but variable. Synthetic media are chemically defined (DMEM, RPMI 1640, MEM, Ham’s F12), usually with 10% serum, or serum-free and protein-free versions.
sa.a_ta: இயற்கை ஊடகங்கள் உயிரியல் திரவங்கள் (பிளாஸ்மா, சீரம், திசுச் சாறுகள், கருச் சாறு); இவை வளமானவை, ஆனால் மாறுபடுபவை. செயற்கை ஊடகங்கள் வேதியியல் ரீதியாக வரையறுக்கப்பட்டவை (DMEM, RPMI 1640, MEM, Ham’s F12); பொதுவாக 10% சீரத்துடன், அல்லது சீரம் அற்ற, புரதம் அற்ற வடிவங்களில் இருக்கும்.

sa.q: Describe the establishment of a primary culture.
sa.a: Collect tissue aseptically, wash in PBS, mince, dissociate with trypsin or collagenase, filter, centrifuge at 200 × g, resuspend in complete medium, count with a haemocytometer and trypan blue (viability ≥ 90%), seed and incubate at 37 °C with 5% CO₂.
sa.a_ta: கிருமியற்ற முறையில் திசுவைச் சேகரித்து, PBS-இல் கழுவி, நறுக்கி, டிரிப்சின் அல்லது கொலாஜனேஸால் பிரித்து, வடிகட்டி, 200 × g-இல் மையவிலக்கி, முழு ஊடகத்தில் மீண்டும் மிதக்கவிட்டு, ஹீமோசைட்டோமீட்டராலும் டிரிப்பான் நீலத்தாலும் எண்ணி (உயிர்ப்புத்திறன் ≥ 90%), விதைத்து 37 °C, 5% CO₂-வில் அடைகாக்கவும்.

sa.q: How are cell lines subcultured and preserved?
sa.a: At 80–90% confluence: wash with PBS, add trypsin-EDTA, neutralise with serum medium, centrifuge, resuspend and split 1:3 to 1:10. For storage: freeze in medium with 10% DMSO at −1 °C/min and keep at −196 °C.
sa.q_ta: செல் வரிசைகள் எவ்வாறு துணை வளர்ப்பு செய்யப்பட்டுப் பாதுகாக்கப்படுகின்றன?
sa.a_ta: 80–90% நிறைவளர்ச்சியில்: PBS-ஆல் கழுவி, டிரிப்சின்-EDTA சேர்த்து, சீரம் ஊடகத்தால் நடுநிலையாக்கி, மையவிலக்கி, மீண்டும் மிதக்கவிட்டு 1:3 முதல் 1:10 வரை பிரிக்கவும். சேமிக்க: 10% DMSO கொண்ட ஊடகத்தில் −1 °C/நிமிடம் என உறைய வைத்து −196 °C-இல் வைக்கவும்.

sa.q: Compare finite and continuous cell lines.
sa.a: Finite lines have a limited life span (~20–50 passages, Hayflick limit) and retain normal diploid features. Continuous lines (HeLa, CHO, Vero) are immortal, often aneuploid and transformed.
sa.a_ta: வரையறுக்கப்பட்ட வரிசைகளுக்குக் குறைந்த ஆயுள் (~20–50 பாசேஜ்கள், ஹேஃப்ளிக் வரம்பு); அவை இயல்பான இருமடிய பண்புகளைத் தக்கவைக்கின்றன. தொடர் வரிசைகள் (HeLa, CHO, Vero) சாகா தன்மை கொண்டவை; பெரும்பாலும் இருமடியற்றவை, உருமாற்றம் அடைந்தவை.

sa.q: Write short notes on ESCs and iPSCs.
sa.a: ESCs come from the blastocyst inner cell mass and are pluripotent; cultured on MEF feeders or Matrigel with LIF (mouse) or bFGF (human). iPSCs are somatic cells reprogrammed with Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc (Yamanaka 2006), avoiding embryo use and allowing autologous therapy.
sa.a_ta: ESC-கள் பிளாஸ்டோசிஸ்டின் உள் செல் திரளிலிருந்து வருபவை; புளூரிபொட்டென்ட் தன்மை கொண்டவை; MEF ஃபீடர்களில் அல்லது மேட்ரிஜெல்லில் LIF (சுண்டெலி) அல்லது bFGF (மனிதன்) உடன் வளர்க்கப்படுகின்றன. iPSC-கள் Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc மூலம் மறுநிரலாக்கப்பட்ட உடல் செல்கள் (யமனகா 2006); கருவைப் பயன்படுத்தாமல், சொந்தச் செல் சிகிச்சையை (ஆட்டோலோகஸ்) இயலச் செய்கின்றன.

sa.q: Explain organ culture and name its methods.
sa.a: Organ culture maintains whole organs or fragments in vitro with their 3-D structure. Methods: watch-glass/plasma clot, grid or raft at the liquid–air interface, perfusion and roller-tube.
sa.q_ta: உறுப்பு வளர்ப்பை விளக்கி, அதன் முறைகளைக் குறிப்பிடுக.
sa.a_ta: உறுப்பு வளர்ப்பு முழு உறுப்புகளையோ துண்டுகளையோ முப்பரிமாணக் கட்டமைப்புடன் இன் விட்ரோ-வில் பேணுகிறது. முறைகள்: கடிகாரக் கண்ணாடி/பிளாஸ்மா உறைவு, திரவ–காற்று இடைமுகத்தில் கட்டம் அல்லது படகு, உட்பாய்ச்சல், சுழல் குழாய்.

sa.q: Describe the production of artificial skin.
sa.a: Keratinocytes from a patient biopsy are expanded; fibroblasts are seeded in a collagen dermal scaffold; keratinocytes are placed on top and cultured at an air–liquid interface for 14–21 days to stratify and cornify; quality is tested before grafting onto burns or ulcers.
sa.a_ta: நோயாளியின் உயிர்த்திசு மாதிரியிலிருந்து கெரட்டினோசைட்டுகள் பெருக்கப்படுகின்றன; கொலாஜன் தோலிடைத் தாங்கு கட்டமைப்பில் ஃபைப்ரோபிளாஸ்ட்கள் விதைக்கப்படுகின்றன; அதன் மேல் கெரட்டினோசைட்டுகள் வைக்கப்பட்டு காற்று–திரவ இடைமுகத்தில் 14–21 நாள்கள் வளர்க்கப்பட்டு அடுக்கமைவும் கெரட்டினாக்கமும் அடைகின்றன; தீப்புண்கள் அல்லது புண்களில் ஒட்டுவதற்கு முன் தரம் சோதிக்கப்படுகிறது.

gl.d: Outside the living organism, for example in a culture flask.
gl.d_ta: உயிருள்ள உயிரினத்துக்கு வெளியே, எடுத்துக்காட்டாக வளர்ப்புக் குடுவையில்.

gl.d: Culture started directly from tissue; finite and heterogeneous.
gl.d_ta: திசுவிலிருந்து நேரடியாகத் தொடங்கிய வளர்ப்பு; வரையறுக்கப்பட்டது, பலவகைமை உடையது.

gl.d: Culture derived by subculturing a primary culture; finite or continuous.
gl.d_ta: முதல்நிலை வளர்ப்பைத் துணை வளர்ப்பு செய்து பெறப்பட்ட வளர்ப்பு; வரையறுக்கப்பட்டதாகவோ தொடர்ச்சியானதாகவோ இருக்கும்.

gl.d: Percentage of the growth surface covered by adherent cells.
gl.d_ta: ஒட்டிவளரும் செல்களால் மூடப்பட்ட வளர்ச்சிப் பரப்பின் சதவீதம்.

gl.d: Transfer of cells to fresh medium and vessels (subculture).
gl.d_ta: செல்களைப் புதிய ஊடகத்துக்கும் கலன்களுக்கும் மாற்றுதல் (துணை வளர்ப்பு).

gl.d: Protease that detaches adherent cells by cleaving surface proteins.
gl.d_ta: மேற்பரப்புப் புரதங்களைப் பிளந்து ஒட்டிவளரும் செல்களைப் பிரிக்கும் புரோட்டியேஸ்.

gl.d: pH indicator in medium: yellow when acidic, pink-red at neutral, purple when alkaline.
gl.d_ta: ஊடகத்திலுள்ள pH நிறங்காட்டி: அமிலமாக இருந்தால் மஞ்சள், நடுநிலையில் இளஞ்சிவப்பு-சிவப்பு, காரமாக இருந்தால் ஊதா.

gl.d: Fetal bovine serum; supplies growth factors, hormones and attachment proteins.
gl.d_ta: மாட்டுக் கருச் சீரம்; வளர்ச்சிக் காரணிகள், இயக்குநீர்கள், ஒட்டுதல் புரதங்களை வழங்குகிறது.

gl.d: Finite number (~50) of divisions of normal somatic cells.
gl.d_ta: இயல்பு உடல் செல்களின் வரையறுக்கப்பட்ட (~50) பிரிவு எண்ணிக்கை.

gl.d: Storage of cells at −196 °C in liquid nitrogen with a cryoprotectant such as DMSO.
gl.d_ta: DMSO போன்ற உறைபாதுகாப்பியுடன் செல்களை −196 °C திரவ நைட்ரஜனில் சேமித்தல்.

gl.d: Able to form all three germ layers.
gl.d_ta: மூன்று கரு அடுக்குகளையும் உருவாக்கும் திறன் கொண்டது.

gl.d: Inactivated cells (for example MEFs) that support growth of stem cells.
gl.d_ta: தண்டு செல்களின் வளர்ச்சியை ஆதரிக்கும் செயலிழக்கச் செய்யப்பட்ட செல்கள் (எ.கா. MEF).

gl.d: Three-dimensional miniature organ-like structure grown from stem cells.
gl.d_ta: தண்டு செல்களிலிருந்து வளர்க்கப்படும் முப்பரிமாண, சிறிய உறுப்பு போன்ற அமைப்பு.

kp_ta: விலங்கு செல் வளர்ப்பு: விலங்குத் திசுவிலிருந்து பிரித்தெடுத்த செல்களைக் கட்டுப்படுத்தப்பட்ட வெப்பநிலை (37 °C), pH (7.2–7.4), CO₂ (5–10%), ஊட்டச்சத்து ஆகியவற்றின் கீழ் இன் விட்ரோ-வில் வளர்த்தல்.
முக்கிய மைல்கற்கள்: ஹாரிசன் 1907 (நரம்பிழை வளர்ப்பு); ஏர்ல் 1943 (எலி ஃபைப்ரோபிளாஸ்ட் செல் வரிசை); HeLa 1951 (முதல் சாகா மனிதச் செல் வரிசை); ஹைப்ரிடோமா 1975; மனித ES செல்கள் 1998; iPSC 2006 (யமனகா).

கிருமிநீக்கம்: ஆட்டோகிளேவ் 121 °C, 15 psi, 15–20 நிமிடம் (ஊடகம், கண்ணாடிப் பொருள்கள்); உலர் வெப்பம் 160–170 °C (கண்ணாடிப் பொருள்கள்); சீரம், வெப்பத்தால் பாதிக்கப்படும் ஊடகங்களுக்கு 0.22 µm வடிகட்டல்; பரப்புகளுக்கு 70% எத்தனால்; பாதுகாப்புப் பெட்டியில் UV 254 nm.
pH-ஐ பீனால் சிவப்பு (மஞ்சள் = அமிலம்) மூலம் கண்காணித்து, பைகார்பனேட் (CO₂-வுடன்) அல்லது HEPES மூலம் தாங்கலாக்குகிறோம்; ஊடுபரவல் அழுத்தம் 280–320 mOsm/kg.
ஊடகங்கள்: இயற்கை (பிளாஸ்மா, சீரம், திசுச் சாறுகள், கருச் சாறு), செயற்கை (DMEM, RPMI 1640, MEM, Ham’s F12); சீரம் அற்ற, புரதம் அற்ற ஊடகங்கள் தொகுதி வேறுபாட்டையும் மாசுபாட்டு ஆபத்தையும் நீக்குகின்றன.

முதல்நிலை வளர்ப்பு: திசுவிலிருந்து நேரடியாக எடுத்த செல்கள் (இயந்திரவழி அல்லது டிரிப்சின்/கொலாஜனேஸ் நொதிவழிப் பிரித்தல்); வரையறுக்கப்பட்ட ஆயுள், பலவகைமை; திசுத் துண்டு வளர்ப்பு – ஒற்றை அடுக்கு வளர்ப்பு.
டிரிப்பான் நீலத் தவிர்ப்பு: உயிருள்ள செல்கள் நிறமற்றவையாக இருக்கும், இறந்த செல்கள் நீலமாகக் கறைபடும்; விதைப்பதற்கு முன் உயிர்ப்புத்திறன் ≥ 90% இருக்க வேண்டும்.

ஒட்டிவளரும் செல்களின் துணை வளர்ப்பு (பாசேஜ்): PBS கழுவல், டிரிப்சின்-EDTA, சீரம் ஊடகத்தால் நடுநிலையாக்கல், 1:3 முதல் 1:10 வரை பிரித்தல்; இயல்பு செல்கள் வரையறுக்கப்பட்டவை (ஹேஃப்ளிக் வரம்பு, ~50 பிரிவுகள்).
தொடர் செல் வரிசைகள்: HeLa (கருப்பை வாய்ப் புற்று), CHO (வெள்ளெலி சூலகம், உயிர்மருந்துகள்), Vero (குரங்கு சிறுநீரகம், தடுப்பூசிகள்), NIH 3T3, MCF-7, Jurkat, PC12.
கிரையோபிரிசர்வேஷன்: ~10% DMSO, −1 °C/நிமிடம் என்ற வீதத்தில் குளிர்வித்தல், −196 °C திரவ நைட்ரஜனில் சேமித்தல்; 37 °C-இல் விரைவாக உருக்கி DMSO-வை நீர்த்தல்.

தண்டு செல்கள்: ESC (புளூரிபொட்டென்ட், உள் செல் திரளிலிருந்து), iPSC (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc), HSC (CD34⁺, எலும்பு மஜ்ஜை மாற்று), MSC (ஆஸ்டியோபிளாஸ்ட்கள், காண்டிரோசைட்டுகள், கொழுப்புச் செல்கள்), NSC (நியூரோஸ்பியர்கள்).
உறுப்பு வளர்ப்பு முப்பரிமாணக் கட்டமைப்பைப் பேணுகிறது: கடிகாரக் கண்ணாடி (ஃபெல், ராபிசன்), கட்டம்/படகு, உட்பாய்ச்சல், சுழல் குழாய் முறைகள்.

செயற்கைத் தோல்: கொலாஜன் தாங்கு கட்டமைப்பின் மீது கெரட்டினோசைட்டுகள் + ஃபைப்ரோபிளாஸ்ட்கள்; அடுக்கமைவுக்கு காற்று–திரவ இடைமுகம்; Apligraf, Integra, Epicel, Dermagraft; வரம்புகள்: இரத்தக் குழாய்கள், நரம்புகள், சுரப்பிகள் இல்லை.
